Lesson 1 · A, An, The — or Nothing
Every
noun
is
a
slot.
Three
questions
tell
you
what
goes
in
it.
Band
5.0
 → 
5.5 · 45 minutes · Focus: Articles and zero article in Part 1 and Part 2 · Theme: Work and future
jobs
Who
this
lesson
is
for: For speakers who leave out articles ('she was Vietnamese teacher'), add them where
they do not belong ('a food', 'on the June'), or decide each one from scratch while speaking.
Start
here
Some languages have no articles at all, so every 'a', 'an' and 'the' in English is a decision made under time
pressure.
Articles are the most frequent small error at Band 5, because every noun is a slot.
Today: one rule in three parts, no long list of exceptions. Then you describe things out loud and count your
slots.
You
need: A phone to record yourself · A timer · Paper and a pen
Warm
up
Answer each question for 30 seconds. Do not worry about articles yet — just talk.
What can you see in the room you are in now?
What subjects are you studying, or did you study at school?
What job would you like to do in the future?
The
rule
The
rule:
A
/
AN
=
ﬁrst
time
or
one
of
many.
THE
=
second
time,
the
only
one,
or
we
both
know
which.
NOTHING
=
plurals
and
uncountables
in
general.
1. Is this the ﬁrst time I mention it, or one of many? →  a / an.
2. Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an app, an engineer, an hour, an instrument.
3. Have I mentioned it before, is it the only one, or do we both know which one? →  the.
4. Am I talking in general, with a plural or an uncountable noun (music, food, maths, clothes)? →  nothing.
5. Do not put a / an before an uncountable noun, and do not stack two determiners ('a some').
Not
yet Better
She was Vietnamese teacher. She was a Vietnamese teacher.
I have never played instrument. I have never played an instrument.
I like a food from my hometown. I like food from my hometown.
I won a some medal at school. I won some medals at school.
My birthday is on the June. My birthday is in June.

Why
it
matters: The public grammar descriptor for Band 5 asks for basic sentence forms 'with reasonable
accuracy'. Articles appear in almost every sentence, so ﬁxing them raises accuracy everywhere at once — and
you already get many 'nothing' slots right.
Practice
Write a, an, the — or a dash (—) for nothing. Then say the sentence out loud and say WHY: ﬁrst time, second
time, only one, or in general.

Timer: 60 seconds each.
25. My room
26. My street
27. A job I would like to do
Upgrade
the
answer
Part 2: a job you would like to do. Read both out loud. Count the article slots in the strong answer.
Weaker
answer: In future, I would like to be software engineer. Software engineer is person who writes
programs for the computers and the phones. Every day, engineer sits at desk, talks with team and ﬁxes
problems in code. I like this job because salary is good. For example, last year I made small game on my
phone. Game was very simple, but my friends played it.
Stronger
answer: That's a good question. In the future, I would like to be a software engineer. A software
engineer is a person who writes programs for computers and phones. Every day, the engineer sits at a desk,
talks with the team and ﬁxes problems in the code. I would like this job for two reasons. First, the salary is
good, so I can help my family. Second, I like solving problems. For example, last year I made a small game on
my phone. The game was very simple, but my friends played it.
First mentions take a / an: a software engineer, a desk, a small game.
Second mentions and things we both know take the: the engineer, the team, the game, the salary.
General plurals and uncountables take nothing: computers, phones, problems.
The sentences are simple, but the articles are right — that is what accuracy at this level sounds like.

Part
3
General ideas often need NO article: people, jobs, money, skills.
Do many people in your country want this kind of job?
Is it diﬃcult to get a good job these days?
What skills will be most important for jobs in the future?
Should schools teach students about diﬀerent jobs?
Moves: Answer (Your view in one sentence.) →  Reason (Because… Watch the general nouns: people, money,
skills.) →  Example (For example, a friend of mine… then 'my friend' or 'he'.) →  Counterpoint (Actually, some
people think…)
Check
your
own
speaking
Record one answer, listen back, count.
Did every singular countable noun have a / an / the (or my, this, etc.)?
Did I switch from a / an to the when I mentioned something again?
Did I avoid a / an with uncountable nouns like food, music, money?
Did I say any phrase twice in a row?
Count: Article slots right ÷ all article slots (a / an / the / nothing).
Finish
and
review
You
can
now:
I can choose a / an, the or nothing and say why.
I can switch from a to the on the second mention.
I can leave out the article for general plurals and uncountables.
I can count my own article slots on a recording.
Next:
Record 60 seconds on 'My room' or 'My street'. Write the ﬁve nouns you used with their articles.
Before you speak, ask the three questions: ﬁrst time? we both know? in general?
Run Part 2 twice (Run A, Run B) on a new card and compare your article counts.

Lesson 15 · Agreement Under Load
Keep
the
-s
right
inside
your
longest,
best
sentences.
Band
6.0
 → 
6.5–7.0 · 50 minutes · Focus: Plural agreement inside complex sentences · Theme: Learning and
change
Who
this
lesson
is
for: For speakers with strong ideas and wide vocabulary who still say 'people has', 'many
person' or 'one of the best teacher' when their sentences get long.
Start
here
Many Band 6 speakers already have Band 7 vocabulary and Band 7 ideas. What keeps the score down is often
one small ending: the -s on a noun or on a verb.
Here is why it matters. Scores of 7, 7, 7 and 6 average 6.75, which rounds up to 7.0. Scores of 7, 7, 7 and 5
average 6.5. One weak criterion costs half a band, so you work on the lowest one.
You probably never make this mistake in short sentences. It hides inside your longest, best sentences, where
you are trying hardest. The mistakes in this lesson are ones Band 6 speakers commonly make, and this lesson
trains agreement exactly where it breaks.
This is not a knowledge problem — it is a production problem. So everything here is said aloud ﬁrst. Reading
the rule again is the least useful thing you could do.
You
need: A phone to record yourself · A timer · A quiet place where you can speak aloud · About 50 minutes
Warm
up
Answer each question aloud for about 30 seconds. Just talk — you will check your endings later.
Who is one of the best teachers you have ever had?
What is one of the biggest changes in your town in recent years?
What is one of the most useful subjects you have ever studied?
What is one of the hardest things about learning English?
Who is one of your closest friends, and what do you do together?
The
rule
The
rule:
A
plural
subject
takes
-s
on
the
noun
and
no
-s
on
the
verb
(people
have,
students
like);
a
singular
subject
takes
no
-s
on
the
noun
and
-s
on
the
verb
(a
person
has,
a
student
likes).
1. Hear the subject ﬁrst: one or many? Fix it in your head — people… people… have — and the verb follows.
2. 'One of the…' has two halves. The noun after it is plural: one of the best teachers. The main verb is singular,
because the subject is one: one of my friends lives abroad.
3. Inside a that or who clause after 'one of the…', the verb goes back to plural: one of the few subjects that
prepare you for work.
4. 'People' is already plural: many people, people have. Never 'many person' or 'people has'.
5. Say the ending loudly enough to hear it. If the examiner cannot hear the -s, it did not happen.
